newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Fallen U.S. airmen honoured by British air museum.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fallen U.S. airmen honoured by British air museum.

text.p: Its black shape scattered terrified villagers as it droned above the jungle in the Vietnam war.
Now the giant B-52 bomber, perhaps the U.S. Air Force's most fearsome warplane, towers over a museum, intimidating visitors with its imposing size.

With its 61-metre (200 feet) wingspan, the bomber is the centre piece of the largest exhibition of U.S. military aircraft in Europe which honours the 30,000 American airmen killed on raids from Britain during World War Two.

"Walking up the ramp, you step virtually straight into the nose of the B-52, the atom bomb carrier, the bomb that could have destroyed the planet," says Simon Reed, an architect closely involved in the project.
"It's ironic, I suppose, because (the B-52) is here to broadcast the museum's commemorative message."
The American Air Museum, housed in a specially-built dome at the Duxford Airfield in eastern England, will be opened by Queen Elizabeth on August 1.

It marks the last resting place of 38 U.S. warplanes ranging from a rickety World War One biplane to a sleek F-111 fighter used in 'Desert Storm' in the 1991 Gulf War. Restored to near their prime, other planes saw action in Korea, Vietnam, in the Cold War and with NATO.
Attending the opening will be Charlton Heston, Hollywood's epic hero, who took part in bombing missions in World War Two from the coast of Alaska.
Heston is the co-chairman of a star-studded campaign that pushed for a British exhibition to pay tribute to Anglo-American co-operation during the War.
James Stewart, the Hollywood legend who died on July 2, was another active supporter.

The 11 million-pound ($18.4 million) project has the blessing of U.S. President Bill Clinton and his predecessors Ronald Reagan and George Bush -- a wartime U.S. Navy pilot in the Pacific -- as well as former British prime ministers John Major and Margaret Thatcher.
Prince Andrew, the queen's second son, recently hosted a $1,000-a-place dinner in New York to raise cash for the museum. He flew helicopters in the Falklands War.
"OVERSEXED AND OVER HERE"
Half a million American servicemen lived in Britain between 1942 and 1945. Some 60,000 married wartime sweethearts while here.
The story goes that the flood of "Yanks" prompted jealous British men to moan that the Americans were "overpaid, over-sexed and over here".
Most U.S. airmen were stationed in eastern England.

Duxford served as a vital Royal Air Force (RAF) base during the 'Battle of Britain'. Later it became the home of the eighth U.S. Air Force division, which flew more than 450 combat missions from here.
The job of the U.S. fighters at Duxford was to escort long range bombers from other bases on their sorties into Germany and enemy-occupied France.
Flying mainly by day, while the RAF flew by night, hundreds of American fliers failed to return from raids on key targets in Dresden, Hamburg and the Ruhr Valley.

"The Americans flew by day being confident they could fight what they could see but often with catastrophic results," says Frank Crosby, a spokesman for the Imperial War Museum which runs the Duxford exhibition.
In addition to American casualties, some 61,000 RAF airmen based in Britain died in the course of World War Two, according to British Ministry of Defence figures.
VETERANS, BRITISH LOTTERY PUT UP CASH

Eleven years in the making, the money for the museum came from British public funds, sponsors and donations by 60,000 American backers, thousands of whom were veterans of British air bases during the war.
Hundreds are flying in to attend the opening.
Of the total, 6.5 million pounds came from Britain's national lottery.

"We nearly didn't get the 8.4 million pounds needed for the building and at times we didn't think it would be built," said David Nelson at British architects Foster and Partners, who were hired to draw up the plans.
The building itself is a talking point.

Sir Norman Foster, one of Britain's most famous architects, designed the dome-like structure. Its main feature is a 295-foot (90-metre) glass front which slices the dome at one end, giving panoramic views of the runway where antique planes still take to the air.
At the entrance, a series of man-sized glass panels have been etched with the shapes of 7,031 aircraft in miniature depicting the known extent of U.S. air losses from Britain during World War Two.
Inside the museum, ramps leading to raised walkways allow visitors to inspect the planes, some of which are suspended from the roof.
Nelson said the size and layout of the museum had been built specifically to accommodate the imposing bulk of the B-52 Stratofortress bomber, the prize exhibit.
Like all the other aircraft in the exhibition, it has been stationed at Duxford for some time and its metal shell had begun to rust badly.
"The form of the B-52 is so beautiful and quiet, we wanted our (building) design to reflect that calm."
Over Vietnam and later in the Gulf War, it was usually the calm before an unforgettable storm. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
